Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_budget_of_China:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/U.S_-_China_-_Russia%2C_Military_Spending.svg/500px-U.S_-_China_-_Russia%2C_Military_Spending.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S_-_China_-_Russia,_Military_Spending.svg)

Military expenditure of China, [Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and [U.S.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") in constant 2021 US$ billions

The **military budget of the People's Republic of China** is the portion of the overall [government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") budget that is allocated for the funding of the [People's Liberation Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army"). This [military budget](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_budget "Military budget") finances employee salaries and training costs, the maintenance of equipment and facilities, support of new or ongoing operations, and development and procurement of new weapons, equipment, and vehicles. Every March, as part of its annual state budget, China releases a single overall figure for national military expenditures. As of 2026, the official military budget was announced to be 1.90 trillion yuan (US$277 billion), the [second largest](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_military_expenditures "List of countries by military expenditures") in the world behind the US.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)

According to the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute"), SIPRI, China was the fourth largest arms exporter in 2019–23 when it accounted for 5.8 per cent of total global arms exports. Its arms exports decreased by 5.3 per cent compared to 2014–18. The bulk of Chinese arms exports (85 per cent) went to states in Asia and Oceania, followed by states in Africa (9.9 per cent). China delivered major arms to 40 states in 2019–23, but well over half of its arms exports (61 per cent) went to just one state—Pakistan.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The Chinese government annually announces the budget for the internal security forces and the PLA at the [National People's Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress") in early March.

* 2014: the budget was announced to be US$131billion.[[10]](#cite_note-auto-10)
* 2015: the budget was announced to be US$141billion.[[11]](#cite_note-11) At the same time, the Chinese government estimated the Chinese economy to grow 7% in 2015.[[12]](#cite_note-12)
* 2016: the budget was announced to be 954.35 billion yuan (US$147 billion), raised 6-7 % above last year's estimates.[[13]](#cite_note-13)
* 2017: the budget was announced to be 1.044 trillion yuan ($151.4 billion), which is an increase of 7% over the last year.[[14]](#cite_note-14)
* 2018: the budget was announced to be 1.11 trillion yuan (US$175 billion), which is an increase of 8.1% over the last year.[[15]](#cite_note-15) This was China's largest defense budget raise in three years.[[16]](#cite_note-16)
* 2019: the budget was announced to be 1.19 trillion yuan (US$176 billion), which is an increase of 7.5% over the last year.
* 2020: the budget was announced to be 1.27 trillion yuan (US$178 billion), which is an increase of 6.6% over the last year.[[17]](#cite_note-17)
* 2021: the budget was announced to be 1.35 trillion yuan (US$209 billion), which is an increase of 6.8% over the last year.[[18]](#cite_note-18)
* 2022: the budget was announced to be 1.45 trillion yuan (US$230 billion), which is an increase of 7.1% over the last year.[[19]](#cite_note-19)
* 2023: the budget was announced to be 1.55 trillion yuan (US$224 billion), which is an increase of 7.2% over the last year.[[20]](#cite_note-:0-20)
* 2024: the budget was announced to be 1.67 trillion yuan (US$231 billion), which is an increase of 7.2% over the last year.[[21]](#cite_note-:1-21)
* 2025: the budget was announced to be 1.78 trillion yuan (US$246 billion), which is an increase of 7.2% over the last year.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)
* 2026: the budget was announced to be 1.91 trillion yuan (US$277 billion), which is an increase of 7% over the last year

## Unofficial estimates

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Military_budget_of_China&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Unofficial estimates")]

Unofficial estimates place the total amount of [military spending](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_spending "Military spending") for China higher than the Chinese government figures, but these calculations tend to differ between organizations.

A [RAND Corporation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAND_Corporation "RAND Corporation") study for year 2003 estimated China's defense spending to be higher than the official number but lower than [United States Department of Defense](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") calculations. The defense spending of China was estimated, in the mid-range estimate, to be 38 billion dollars or 2.3% of China's [GDP](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") in 2003. The official figure was 22.4 billion dollars. Nevertheless, Chinese military spending doubled between 1997 and 2003, nearly reaching the level of the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), and it continued to grow over 10% annually during 2003–2005.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

In 2010, the US Department of Defense's annual report to Congress on China's military strength estimated the actual 2009 Chinese military spending at US$150 billion.[[23]](#cite_note-DOD-23) [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIPRI "SIPRI") estimates that the military spending of the People's Republic of China for 2009 was US$100 billion,[[24]](#cite_note-24) higher than the official budget, but lower than the US DoD estimate.

The [International Institute for Strategic Studies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Institute_for_Strategic_Studies "International Institute for Strategic Studies") in a 2011 report argued that if spending trends continue China will achieve military equality with the United States in 15–20 years.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

[Jane's Defence Forecasts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane's_Information_Group "Jane's Information Group") in 2012 estimated that China's defense budget would increase from $119.80 billion to $238.20 billion between 2011 and 2015. This would make it larger than the defense budgets of all other major Asian nations combined. This is still smaller than the estimated United States defense budget of $525.40 billion for 2013. However, United States defense spending is slightly declining.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In 2017, the magazine [Popular Mechanics](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mechanics "Popular Mechanics") estimated that China's annual military spending is greater than $200 billion, around 2% of the GDP.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In 2019, Peter Robertson, a professor from the [University of Western Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Australia "University of Western Australia"), argued that using conventional currency conversion as opposed to more accurate "purchasing power parity" (PPP) exchange rates dramatically understated China's military capabilities and that China's real military spending was equivalent to US spending of $455 billion, calculated from a [PPP](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") perspective.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In 2023, the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute") estimated the China's military spending is $296 billion which accounted for 1.7% of the country total GDP. [[29]](#cite_note-29)

A 2024 study by [Taylor Fravel](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Fravel "Taylor Fravel"), George J. Gilboy, and Eric Heginbotham estimated China's total military spending for 2024 at US$471 billion.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

# Lens 2B.8 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler use military spending and mobilization to meet real security needs, or to enrich networks, reward security elites, intimidate neighbors, or project personal strength?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** on the question of whether military spending and mobilization served real security needs rather than network-enrichment, elite-reward, intimidation, or personal-strength projection. China announced a 7.2% defense-budget increase to ¥1.55 trillion (US$224B official / SIPRI-estimated US$296B) in 2023, exceeding official GDP growth (5.2%); the spending occurred against a backdrop of continued grey-zone coercion against the Philippines, no binding South China Sea Code of Conduct, maximalist Taiwan posture absent defensive trigger, ICBM silo construction in Gansu / Xinjiang, PLARF social-media normalization of nuclear-strike videos, and a PLARF leadership purge framed in loyalty-and-corruption terms — i.e., the spending was directed at intimidation, projection, and elite-loyalty-reward rather than at meeting verifiable real security needs.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — 2023 defense spending scale and trajectory

### 1. Official 2023 defense budget: ¥1.55 trillion, +7.2% YoY, exceeding official GDP growth

- **Claim A1.** In March 2023, the Chinese government announced a 2023 defense budget of 1.55 trillion yuan (US$224 billion at official rates), a 7.2% increase over 2022. This exceeded the official 2023 GDP growth rate of 5.2%. SIPRI estimated real 2023 Chinese military spending at US$296 billion (~1.7% of GDP). A 2024 study by Taylor Fravel, George J. Gilboy, and Eric Heginbotham estimated China's total 2024 military spending at US$471 billion (using PPP), suggesting 2023 actual was higher than the official ¥1.55T figure.
  - **Source:** "Military budget of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_budget_of_China ("2023: the budget was announced to be 1.55 trillion yuan (US$224 billion), which is an increase of 7.2% over the last year").
  - **Source:** "In 2023, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated the China's military spending is $296 billion which accounted for 1.7% of the country total GDP."
  - **Source:** "2023_in_China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (linked 5.2% GDP growth).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — spending growth exceeds GDP growth without defensive-need justification), 8B, 1B.1.

### 2. Continuation of multi-year nuclear / conventional buildup

- **Claim A2.** The 2023 budget was consumed in a multi-year pattern of: stockpile growth from ~410 to ~500 warheads, continued ICBM silo construction in Gansu/Yumen and additional fields (10x pre-2021 baseline), continued triad buildout (DF-series ICBMs, JL-3 SLBMs, H-6N ALBMs, Type 094/096 SSBNs), continued development of the H-20 stealth bomber and Type 096 SSBN, and continued movement toward launch-on-warning posture. The pattern is not a one-year spike but a sustained, multi-year direction-of-travel.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal and is projected to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030 and up to ~1,500 by 2035 … China is upgrading its triad with the in-development Xi'an H-20 stealth bomber, Type 096 submarine, and large missile silo fields … Some of its nuclear forces are reported to have moved toward a launch on warning (LOW) posture").
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("The Chinese stockpile is increasing").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — direction-of-travel is projection, not defensive-need satisfaction), 1B.1, 1B.5.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — spending and mobilization directed at intimidation, projection, and elite reward

### 3. PLARF leadership purge in 2023 — used as anti-corruption loyalty instrument, not defensive-security reform

- **Claim A3.** Between July and October 2023, the entire top of China's nuclear-rocket force was rotated simultaneously: PLARF commander Li Yuchao and deputy commander Liu Guangbin removed; political commissar replaced; replacements Wang Houbin (Navy) and Xu Xisheng (Air Force political work) brought in from outside the branch — "extremely rare" per SCMP. Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared in August and was removed 24 October. The CMC's anti-corruption framing of these changes prioritized loyalty over nuclear-strategic competence, and the SCMP/Wikipedia flagged explicit concerns about "the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA." The pattern is consistent with using the defense apparatus as an instrument of personal-control and elite-reward rather than for defensive security.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *South China Morning Post*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal ("It is extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force's commander and its political chief at the same time").
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force ("it was thought to be an odd decision to replace the Rocket Force commander with military personnel from outside the branch, and this led to concerns about the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA").
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu.
  - **Source:** "Li Yuchao" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — elite reward / loyalty filter), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 4. PLARF 2023 social-media nuclear-strike videos — intimidation, not defensive

- **Claim A4.** In August–September 2023, PLARF-linked official-media accounts posted animated simulations of nuclear strikes on US territory and Taiwan-related targets. The videos were later removed after Western press attention, but Xi did not publicly repudiate them. The 2023 defense-budget allocation to PLARF continued at a high level alongside this normalization-of-use messaging. The pattern is consistent with intimidation rather than defensive security.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ (references the broader 2023 PLARF system-rhetoric on nuclear use).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — intimidation use), 1B.2, 1B.5, 2B.3.

### 5. Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis continued — operational coercion without defensive trigger

- **Claim A5.** Throughout 2023, the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis continued with PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, naval patrols, and Coast Guard boardings. Taiwan did not attack China, did not declare independence in 2023, and did not provoke the PLA exercises. The 2023 defense spending supported this grey-zone coercion campaign. The pattern is consistent with intimidation and projection rather than defensive response.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis.
  - **Source:** "2023 in Taiwan" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Taiwan (no 2023 Taiwanese provocation).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — projection / intimidation), 1B.5, 1B.4, 2B.3.

### 6. South China Sea grey-zone coercion against the Philippines

- **Claim B6.** Throughout 2023, China's grey-zone coercion against the Philippines continued, with the 10 November 2023 "control measures" against Philippine vessels at Second Thomas Shoal a representative incident. The 2023 spending supported this coast-guard and maritime-militia operational pattern. No binding COC, no defensive trigger.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry).
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — intimidation of neighbors), 1B.5, 1B.4, 2B.3.

### 7. He Weidong in January 2024 — loyalty-first discipline framing

- **Claim B7.** In January 2024 (representative of 2023 CMC discourse), CMC Vice-Chairman He Weidong called on the CMC discipline commission to "maintain loyalty and support to CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping," to "adhere to a strict tone, use stricter standards to scrutinize the key few, and show determination to get to the bottom of long-standing [corruption] problems." This is personal-control framing, not defensive-security framing.
  - **Source:** "He Weidong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Weidong ("considered to have been a part of the Fujian clique of the Xi Jinping faction within the CCP … He also called on the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection to maintain loyalty and support to CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — personal control framing), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4.

### 8. Patrotic Education Law (October 2023) — uses defense / national-security narrative for regime legitimacy

- **Claim B8.** The Patriotic Education Law signed by Xi on 24 October 2023 mandates patriotic education across all levels and types of schooling, requires internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content, and explicitly extends to Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and overseas Chinese. Article 33 mandates internet platforms to develop "new technologies and products to vividly carry out patriotic education activities." The mandatory content includes Xi Jinping Thought. The 2023 use of defense / national-security narrative as a regime-legitimacy instrument is consistent with projection rather than defensive security.
  - **Source:** "Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — projection / legitimacy), 2B.3, 2B.6.

### 9. BRI Forum hosting of Putin (October 2023) — military-budget support for partner legitimation

- **Claim B9.** On 17–18 October 2023, Xi hosted Putin at the 3rd Belt and Road Forum in Beijing and provided a high-profile platform for Putin's first meeting with an EU leader (Hungarian PM Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The 2023 Chinese military-budget framework supported a strategic posture that included platforming of a partner pursuing a nuclear-coercion campaign in Ukraine. This is partner-legitimation, not defensive security.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — partner legitimation), 1B.6, 2B.3.

### 10. PLA mobilization tempo vs. real security need

- **Claim B10.** In 2023, no new international armed conflict required a Chinese military response; the LAC standoff did not produce 2023 kinetic engagements comparable to 2020 Galwan; the Taiwan operational pressure remained grey-zone rather than kinetic. The 7.2% real-terms defense-budget increase cannot be justified by a real 2023 security need in the standard counter-factual sense; it served projection and intimidation.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Source:** "China–India relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93India_relations (no 2023 LAC kinetic engagement).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — no real security need), 1B.4, 8G.

### 11. The "Western containment" framing as defense-budget justification

- **Claim B11.** Throughout 2023, Xi's official speeches consistently framed China as facing "Western containment" and "hegemony." The 2023 defense-budget growth was presented in this context. The threat frame is selectively amplified: real US export controls, AUKUS, and NATO expansion are real, but they do not justify a 7.2% real-terms defense-budget increase against an economy growing 5.2%, especially in a year without major territorial defense requirements.
  - **Source:** "Third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Belt_and_Road_Forum_for_International_Cooperation.
  - **Source:** "Military budget of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_budget_of_China (the 7.2% increase is a 4-decade consistent pattern).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — selective threat-amplification), 2B.3, 2B.6, 8G.

### 12. Civilian-procurement co-option — no 2023 institutional anti-corruption reform

- **Claim B12.** Throughout 2023, the anti-corruption campaign continued to be the primary instrument through which Xi removed senior officials (PLARF commander July 2023, defense minister October 2023, 9 NPC military delegates December 2023). The campaign was a personal-control instrument, not a state-capacity reform: the 2023 replacements were drawn from outside the nuclear-rocket branch (Navy, Air Force political work, Army ground force from Xi's "Fujian clique"). No civilian-expert track or independent anti-corruption institution was created in 2023.
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu (cites the NPC Gazette: "serious violation of discipline and law").
  - **Source:** "He Weidong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Weidong (Fujian clique).
  - **Source:** "Wang Houbin" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Houbin.
  - **Source:** "China Ousts Nine Military Lawmakers as Defense Purge Widens," *Bloomberg News*, 29 December 2023 — https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-12-29/china-s-legislature-ousts-nine-military-cadres-as-turmoil-widens.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — personal control, not state-capacity reform), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 13. The PLARF structure: command + political commissar replaced simultaneously

- **Claim B13.** The 31 July 2023 simultaneous replacement of PLARF commander and political commissar is described by SCMP as "extremely rare." The fact that both were replaced at once, and that the replacements came from outside the branch, is a structural pattern: not routine rotation, but a direct Xi-directed personnel action. The 2023 spending pattern followed — i.e., the spending was directed by Xi via a personal-loyalty personnel filter, not by an institutional defensive-security process.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *SCMP*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (negative — personal direction of defense apparatus), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4.

---

## C. Claim-level findings — partial restraint positives

### 14. November 2023 Biden–Xi mil-to-mil reset

- **Claim C1.** The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit produced an explicit agreement to **resume US-China military-to-military communications**, suspended since August 2022. This is a channel-preservation positive that reduces inadvertent-escalation risk — a defensive-security rationale.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (positive — defensive-security CBM), 1B.8, 8G.3.

### 15. No 2023 kinetic war initiated

- **Claim C2.** In 2023, China did not initiate any new international armed conflict. No new border war, no new invasion, no new air or naval campaign beyond the operational pattern already established by the August 2022 PLA exercises around Taiwan. The 2023 budget supported the existing operational pattern but did not initiate new kinetic action.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (positive — no new war), 1B.1, 2B.2, 8G.

### 16. NFU reaffirmation at the Biden–Xi summit

- **Claim C3.** At the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit, Xi reaffirmed China's unconditional no-first-use nuclear posture. This is a defensive-security restraint norm.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.8 (positive — defensive restraint norm), 1B.2, 1B.10.

---

## D. Net reading for lens 2B.8

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** on the question of whether military spending and mobilization served real security needs vs. network-enrichment, elite-reward, intimidation, or personal-strength projection:

- **Spending scale:** ¥1.55 trillion (US$224B official / SIPRI US$296B) defense budget in 2023, +7.2% YoY, exceeding official GDP growth of 5.2%.
- **Spending direction:** continued stockpile growth, silo construction, triad buildout, LOW posture — a sustained multi-year projection pattern.
- **Spending accompanied by:** PLARF leadership purge (loyalty filter); PLARF nuclear-strike social-media videos; Taiwan operational coercion without defensive trigger; South China Sea grey-zone against Philippines; BRI hosting of Putin; Patriotic Education Law using national-security narrative for regime legitimacy; selective amplification of "Western containment" framing.
- **Spending NOT accompanied by:** institutional anti-corruption reform; civilian-expert track; nuclear-safety program; 2023 transparency; arms-control engagement; cross-strait or India LAC disengagement; partner correction on atrocities; CTBT ratification.
- **Positive restraint items:** November 2023 mil-to-mil reset, NFU reaffirmation, no new kinetic war.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) coupled the 7.2% defense-budget increase with a public defensive-need justification (e.g., specific threat-actor behavior), (b) shifted the spending mix from gray-zone coercion to defensive-resilience, (c) coupled the PLARF leadership purge with a parallel nuclear-safety reform program, (d) refrained from the PLARF nuclear-strike social-media videos, (e) used the BRI Forum as a platform for restraint rather than Putin legitimation. Xi did the opposite on each.

**Net judgment: 2B.8 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi used the 7.2% real-terms defense-budget increase to project personal strength, intimidate neighbors, and consolidate security-elite loyalty through a personal-loyalty filter, rather than to meet verifiable real security needs. The PLARF nuclear-strike social-media normalization, BRI hosting of Putin, and maximalist Taiwan posture are the most explicit 2023 projection uses.**

---
